title: One client for everything
scenario: A company is building an internal assistant for its staff. It will use MCP to reach three systems: the code repository, the HR database and a web search service. A junior engineer wrote the first design note (exhibit). You review it before any server is built.
exhibit:
DESIGN NOTE v0.1 (made-up example)

Host:   staff-assistant (desktop app)
Client: one shared MCP client, connected to all three servers

Servers:
  repo-server    local process   (files, git history)
  hr-server      remote service  (HR database)
  search-server  remote service  (web search)

Open requests from the server teams:
  hr-server team: "Send us the full conversation on every
  call, so our answers have more context."

Planned features:
  F1  /weekly-report      user picks it from the slash menu
  F2  HR policy document  app attaches it as context
  F3  create_ticket       model decides when to call it

Safety: "The MCP protocol enforces user consent, so the
host needs no consent screens."

questions.prompt: The note plans one shared MCP client for all three servers. What does the spec's architecture say?

options.text: One client is right, because a host may run only one client.
options.explanation: The spec says the opposite: each host can run multiple client instances.

options.text: The host should create one client per server; each client talks to exactly one server.
options.explanation: Right. The architecture page says each client communicates with exactly one server, a 1:1 relationship.

options.text: Remote servers need a client each, but local servers can share one.
options.explanation: The 1:1 rule does not depend on where the server runs. Local and remote servers each get their own client.

options.text: Clients are optional; the host can talk to servers directly.
options.explanation: In the spec, clients are the connectors inside the host. The host reaches each server through a client.

questions.prompt: The HR server team wants the full conversation on every call. What fits MCP's design principles?

options.text: Agree, because MCP servers always receive the whole chat history.
options.explanation: The spec says servers should not be able to read the whole conversation. They are not sent it by default.

options.text: Agree, but only for remote servers, which have no other context.
options.explanation: Being remote does not change the principle. Remote or local, servers get only the context they need.

options.text: Let the HR server read the repo server's data instead of the chat.
options.explanation: The spec says servers should not 'see into' other servers. Cross-server interactions are controlled by the host.

options.text: Refuse: full history stays with the host, and the server gets only the context it needs.
options.explanation: Right. The architecture page: servers receive only necessary contextual information, and full conversation history stays with the host.

questions.prompt: Which mapping of F1, F2 and F3 to MCP primitives matches the spec's control model?

options.text: F1 prompt, F2 resource, F3 tool
options.explanation: Right. Prompts are user-controlled (slash commands), resources are application-controlled (context the app attaches), tools are model-controlled.

options.text: F1 tool, F2 prompt, F3 resource
options.explanation: A user-picked slash command is the spec's example of a prompt, and a function the model decides to call is a tool.

options.text: F1 resource, F2 tool, F3 prompt
options.explanation: A document the app attaches is a resource. A prompt is chosen by the user, not called by the model.

options.text: All three should be tools, because only tools reach the model.
options.explanation: Resources and prompts also put content into the model's context. The difference is who decides when they are used.

questions.prompt: The note says the protocol enforces consent, so the host needs no consent screens. What is the problem?

options.text: None: MCP servers ask the user for consent before every tool call.
options.explanation: The spec puts consent on the host: hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool.

options.text: Consent is the model's job, so the system prompt must ask for it.
options.explanation: The spec gives this job to the host application, not to the model.

options.text: MCP cannot enforce it at the protocol level; the host must get explicit consent before invoking tools.
options.explanation: Right. The spec says MCP itself cannot enforce these security principles, and hosts must obtain explicit user consent before invoking any tool.

options.text: Consent is only needed for local servers, which can touch files.
options.explanation: The consent principles in the spec do not depend on where the server runs.
